report:
The health claim is **supported by medical consensus and clinical evidence**, though specific trial results explain why some skepticism exists.

### Evidence Supporting the Claim
Major global guidelines—including those from the World Health Organization (WHO)—recommend tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) starting in the third trimester (28–32 weeks) for pregnant women with high hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA levels (≥200,000 IU/mL). A landmark clinical trial published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* (Pan et al., 2016) showed that third-trimester TDF significantly reduced mother-to-child transmission compared to infant immunoprophylaxis alone (0% vs. 7% per-protocol transmission).

### Origin of Skepticism
Doubts regarding TDF's necessity often cite a 2018 clinical trial in Thailand (Jourdain et al., 2018). In that study, when infants received hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) immediately at birth alongside prompt vaccination, transmission was exceptionally low in both groups (0% with TDF vs. 2% with placebo), yielding a statistically non-significant difference.

### Conclusion
While infant immunoprophylaxis alone is effective under ideal clinical conditions, immunoprophylaxis failures still occur in women with very high viral loads. Thus, medical consensus recommends third-trimester tenofovir to minimize transmission risk.

### Sources
* Pan et al., NEJM Trial (2016): https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1508660
* NIH Summary of Thailand Trial (2018): https://stagetestdomain5.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/antiviral-drug-not-beneficial-reducing-mother-child-transmission-hepatitis-b-when-added-existing-preventatives
* World Health Organization Hepatitis B Fact Sheet: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hepatitis-b
